terms.def: The earliest phase of a project, where the team defines what the game is, who it is for and why it will stand out. It usually ends with a pitch or a greenlight decision.
A formal decision by studio leadership or a publisher to move a project into its next phase, most often from concept or pre-production into full production.

The phase where a team proves the game is fun and feasible before committing to full production: prototyping core mechanics, settling art direction and technology, and planning the work. It often ends with a vertical slice.
A quick, rough build made to answer one question, such as whether a mechanic is fun, with no expectation that its code or art will survive into the final game.
A level built from simple, untextured shapes to test layout, scale and flow before final art is made. Also called a whitebox or blockout.
The first build in which a player can experience the core loop from start to finish, however rough it looks.
A short section of the game built to near-final quality in every discipline, from gameplay to art, audio and UI. It proves the quality bar and is often used to secure funding.

link.text: Where the vertical slice fits in a roadmap

terms.def: The longest phase of development, in which the team builds the game's features and content against milestones.

The milestone at which the game is usually feature complete: every planned feature exists and works in some form, though content may be missing and bugs remain. Studios define alpha differently, so write the criteria down.
The point at which every planned feature is implemented. After it, no new features go in, only content, fixes and polish. Often the same milestone as alpha.
The point at which all planned content, such as levels, assets, dialogue and audio, is in the game, even if it still needs polish. Often tied to beta.
The milestone at which the game is usually content complete and the team's focus shifts to fixing bugs, performance and polish.
The point after which only approved fixes may be checked in, so the build can stabilize for release or certification. Also called code freeze.
A build the team believes is ready to ship, submitted for final testing or platform certification. Often shortened to RC.
The final approved build that ships. "Going gold" historically meant sending the build for disc manufacturing.
An update released at or near launch to fix issues found after the gold build was locked.
A defined point in a project with agreed deliverables and acceptance criteria, often tied to a publisher payment.

link.text: How to write a milestone document

terms.def: The specific, testable conditions a deliverable or milestone must meet to be accepted. Also called exit criteria when they apply to a whole milestone.
A high-level plan of what will be built and when, at the level of milestones and major features. It changes deliberately, unlike the schedule.
The plan for what new content a game releases after launch, and when: seasons, events, updates and new modes. It is the central planning document for live-service games.
The detailed plan of who does what and when, at task level. Unlike the roadmap, it changes constantly.
The longest chain of dependent tasks in a project. Any delay on the critical path delays the whole project.
A task or deliverable that cannot start or finish until another one does, such as animation waiting on a finished character rig.
Time deliberately held in the schedule for problems no individual task predicts, such as integration issues or a failed certification pass.
A bar chart that shows tasks against time, with their dependencies. Often used for milestone-level schedules.
The total set of features and content a project commits to deliver.

link.text: How to scope a game realistically

terms.def: Gradual growth in a project's scope without matching changes to its schedule or budget. Feature creep is the same problem applied to features.
A ranked list of features or content that will be removed first if the project runs short of time or money.
The amount of work a team can realistically take on in a period, after holidays, meetings, support work and other commitments.
How much money a studio or project spends per month.
How long a studio can keep operating before it runs out of money at its current burn rate.
Extended periods of mandatory or expected overtime. It is most often a symptom of planning and scope problems, and is widely documented as harmful to people and to quality.
A family of iterative approaches that plan in short cycles and adapt as the team learns, rather than fixing every detail up front.
An agile framework built around fixed-length sprints, with three roles (product owner, Scrum Master and developers) and set events such as planning, daily scrum, review and retrospective.
A fixed period, one month or less and often two weeks, in which a team commits to a set of work.
In Scrum, the person accountable for ordering the backlog and deciding what the team works on next.
The ordered list of work that has not started yet.
A short description of a feature from the player's point of view, with acceptance criteria that say when it is done.
A large body of work broken down into smaller stories.
A relative measure of effort used to estimate backlog items by comparing them with each other rather than in hours.
The amount of work, usually in story points, a team completes per sprint. Useful for forecasting within one team, not for comparing teams or individuals.
A chart that shows the work remaining against time in a sprint or milestone.
The shared checklist a piece of work must satisfy before it counts as finished, such as reviewed, integrated, tested and in the build.
A short daily meeting where team members share progress, plans and blockers.
A regular meeting where a team reviews how it worked and commits to specific improvements.
A flow-based method that visualizes work on a board and limits work in progress, without fixed-length sprints.
A cap on how many items can be in one stage of a Kanban board at once, which exposes bottlenecks.
A list of things that could go wrong on a project, each with a probability, impact, owner, mitigation and contingency.
Action taken before a risk occurs to make it less likely or less damaging.
What the team will do if a risk happens anyway.
Deciding, for each incoming bug, whether it reproduces, how severe and urgent it is, and who owns it.
How bad a bug's effect is, from crashes and data loss down to cosmetic issues. It is separate from priority.
How soon a bug will be fixed relative to other work. A low-severity bug can be high priority, and the reverse.
A bug in something that used to work, introduced by a later change.
A quick check that a new build's most basic functions work before deeper testing begins.
Running a build for an extended period to find crashes, memory leaks and other problems that only appear over time.
A session where players try the game while the team observes what is fun, confusing or broken.

link.text: QA and playtesting for indie games

terms.def: A review after a project or milestone of what went right, what went wrong and what to change next time.
A platform holder's testing of a console game against its technical requirements before the game may be released. Often shortened to cert.
Sony's Technical Requirements Checklist, the certification requirements for PlayStation releases.
Xbox Requirements, Microsoft's certification requirements for Xbox releases.
Nintendo's certification process for games released on its platforms.
A content rating from a ratings body such as the ESRB in North America or PEGI in Europe, required by most storefronts.
The International Age Rating Coalition, which issues age ratings for digital games through a single questionnaire used by participating storefronts.
Adapting a game for other languages and regions. Localization QA, or LQA, checks the translated text in context in the game.
Valve's process for publishing a game on Steam, with a $100 fee per game that Valve returns once the game earns $1,000 in adjusted gross revenue.
A Steam store page published before release so players can wishlist the game. Valve requires it to be live for at least two weeks before launch.

link.text: Building a Steam page that converts

terms.def: A Steam player's saved interest in a game. Steam notifies wishlisters when the game launches and when it gets a qualifying discount.
A Steam event, held several times a year, where players try free demos of upcoming games.

link.text: Steam sale and Next Fest calendar

terms.def: Selling an unfinished game while development continues, with player feedback shaping the full release.
Releasing a game in a limited set of markets before the global launch to test stability, retention and monetization. Most common in mobile.
Running a game after launch: releasing content and events, watching the game's health and economy, and responding to incidents.
A fixed-length period of content and progression in a live game, often paired with a battle pass.
A tiered reward track players progress through during a season, usually with free and paid tiers.
An urgent fix deployed outside the normal release cadence.
Daily and monthly active users. The ratio of the two is a common measure of how often players come back.
The share of players who return after their first session, usually measured at day 1, day 7 and day 30 (D1, D7 and D30).
The number of players online at the same time. Peak concurrent users, or peak CCU, is a common health metric.
Average revenue per daily active user.
The total revenue a player is expected to generate over their time with the game. Often shortened to LTV.
A company that funds, markets or distributes a game in exchange for a share of its revenue, and often some rights.
Money a publisher pays a developer before release, usually against milestones, and usually recouped from the developer's royalties.
A publisher recovering agreed costs, such as advances and marketing, from a game's revenue before royalties are paid.
The developer's share of revenue under a publishing deal, typically paid after recoupment.
Paying people or partners a percentage of revenue instead of, or as well as, a fee.
The share of each sale a store keeps. Steam's standard share is 30%, falling to 25% and then 20% at high lifetime revenue.
The ownable parts of a game, such as its world, characters, code, art and trademarks. Often shortened to IP.
A legal arrangement in which the commissioning party owns a work from the moment it is created. In the US it applies to contractors only in specific circumstances and must be agreed in writing.
A non-disclosure agreement, which protects confidential information shared during pitches, contracts or playtests.
Non-repayable public or private funding for game development, usually awarded competitively against criteria such as cultural value or location.
A rebate of a share of eligible development spending, claimed through the tax system by studios that meet a program's rules.
The person who owns how and when the game gets made: planning, coordination, risk and making sure decisions get made.
An early-career production role focused on tracking work, coordinating between disciplines and supporting a producer.
An experienced producer who owns a large part of a project, or a whole smaller one, often managing other producers.
A senior production leader accountable for a whole project or portfolio, often owning the budget and key stakeholder relationships.
A producer who specializes in engineering coordination, build pipelines and technical risk.
A compiled, playable version of the game.
The automated system that compiles, packages and distributes builds. Continuous integration (CI) builds and tests every change as it is committed.
Software that tracks every change to code and assets, such as Perforce or Git.
A separate line of development in version control, used to isolate work such as a release or a risky feature.
The shared description of what the game is and how it works. Often shortened to GDD, and best kept short and current.
The software framework a game is built on, providing rendering, physics, audio, input and tools, such as Unity, Unreal or Godot.
Any piece of content used in the game, such as a model, texture, sound, animation or UI element.
